\section[vesper]{vesper — the evening word its own daughters mostly abandoned}

\label{lesson:LA-C33-vesper}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} A genuinely ordinary Latin word for "evening" — and a root that quietly reaches all the way to the English word \emph{west}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Vesper} (also \textbf{vespera}) — "\textbf{evening}" — is a genuine, ordinary Classical Latin word, not a rare or poetic one: \textbf{vespere} ("in the evening") shows up routinely in Cicero's own letters. It traces to \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*wekero-}} ("evening, night"), itself an enlarged form of a root \emph{\textbf{*we-}}, which some reconstructions gloss as "down" (the direction the sun sets) — though this specific piece is more contested than the vesper/west link itself. That same conceptual root, through a completely separate \textbf{Germanic} branch, gives English its own word for "\textbf{west}" — evening and west, sharing one deep idea: the direction the sun goes down.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "vesper" — "evening," genuinely everyday Classical Latin{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the deep root — \emph{wekero-}, shared with English "west," the direction of sunset{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the careful hedge — a lower root meaning "down" is more contested{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What English word shares vesper's deep PIE root, and what's the connecting idea? (\textbf{West} — both trace to the direction the sun sets.) Is the proposed still-deeper root meaning "down" equally secure? (\textbf{No — that sub-root is more contested than the vesper/west link.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Hesperia, víspera, vespers]{Hesperia, víspera, vespers — the root after Latin}

\label{lesson:LA-C33-vesper-afterlives}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Latin \textbf{vesper} and English \textbf{west} share the sunset idea. Now follow the evening root through Greek, English, Spanish, French, and Italian.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Greek hesperos}
The Greek cognate \textbf{hesperos} gives English \textbf{Hesperus}, the evening star (Venus at dusk), and \textbf{Hesperia}, "land of the west." The name is relative: Greeks used it for Italy, west of Greece; Romans could use it for Spain, west of Italy.

\begin{cousinweb}
English borrowed \textbf{vespers}, the evening prayer service, and \textbf{vespertine}, "of the evening," directly from Latin.

Spanish inherited \emph{vespera} as \textbf{víspera}, but narrowed its meaning to "the eve" or "the day before" an event. French \textbf{soir} and Italian \textbf{sera} do not descend from \textbf{vesper} at all. They rebuilt "evening" from Latin \textbf{sērus}, "late," through the idea of the "late day."

One ordinary Latin word therefore leaves three different outcomes: a learned English loan, a narrowed Spanish descendant, and replacement by a different root in French and Italian.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "Hesperia" — land of the west{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "víspera" — the eve or day before, narrowed from evening{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "soir, sera" — from sērus, "late," not from vesper{]}
\end{itemize}
